Were losing all our Strong Female Characters to Trinity Syndrome

I liked the article - to quote a few lines:

It’s hard for any action movie to have two or more equal heroes, and the ensemble approach doesn’t work for every story.

This seems to be the crux of it. If producers and writers shoehorn in a Strong Female Character just to keep the SJWs at bay, then the new problem it creates (competition for the hero spotlight) will ultimately relegate her to a sideline once she's said her piece.

The conclusion of the article is particularly well written:

So maybe all the questions can boil down to this: Looking at a so-called Strong Female Character, would you—the writer, the director, the actor, the viewer—want to be her? Not want to prove you’re better than her, or to have her praise you or acknowledge your superiority. Action movies are all about wish-fulfillment. Does she fulfill any wishes for herself, rather than for other characters? When female characters are routinely “strong” enough to manage that, maybe they’ll make the “Strong Female Characters” term meaningful enough that it isn’t so often said sarcastically.

Male roles are often about empowerment fantasy, so as writers maybe we can take a few notes from that approach? If I were a better writer maybe I'd have more to say, but I still enjoyed the article. Good stuff!

I can't help feeling that using "Edge of Tomorrow" as an example of what movies should be striving for isn't really the best example.

Towards the end (and even at the beginning, before what's happening is revealed) Rita is entirely dependent on Cage's memory of the day to survive past the initial landing. So much so that Cage then admits that she is the sole reason he's been unable to advance past a certain point, because she always dies, and he loves her. Essentially making the only point of her character a ball-and-chain love interest.

She's perhaps the epitome of "Trinity Syndrome".

I didn't get that vibe at all. If anything Cage was the ball and chain dragging her down. Yes, she had to rely on his memory but she had to train him to be half the badass she was just so she could get things done. You could see her frustration throughout the movie that if she still had the ability, she would have ended this so easily. Instead she's forced to drag him along for his main redeeming quality (the ability to remember).

She was also the one who gave him the most shit about putting his feelings before the mission. In my mind she was the hero of the story and he was simply the tool she used to finish the job.

The fact remains that you could remove Rita from the movie completely, and it'd be relatively unchanged. Without Cage intervening, Rita dies seconds after landing every time. If she doesn't do exactly what Cage says, when he says it, she dies. Her only real contribution, where she was the only person who could have done it, was introducing Cage to the doctor whose name I forget.

Every other event she was included in, her character was irrelevant. Training? He could have gotten better over time. Distracting the alpha at the end? Could have been any other nameless grunt Cage took with him. Motivation for Cage? Instead of being in love with Rita, he just wants to win.

Remove her from the movie and there's only 1 gap (that I can remember), and it's only because she knows a dude Cage wouldn't have met otherwise.

This is Trinity Syndrome à la The Matrix: the hugely capable woman who never once becomes as independent, significant, and exciting as she is in her introductory scene.

The article doesn't define what it's actually about until halfway through. This combined with the lack of a real thesis sentence makes the article lack any kind of punch.
